source_lines.24: For a nonnegative integer $q$, let $M=2^q$, set $\omega=1$ when $M=1$ and $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ when $M>1$, and let $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_{M-1})\in\mathbb C^M$. The forward discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is the vector $\widehat a\in\mathbb C^M$ with $\widehat a_k=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}a_j\omega^{jk}$. The radix-two procedure returns this vector by the following exact recursion. If $M=1$, return $(a_0)$. If $M>1$, recursively compute the length-$M/2$ DFTs $E$ and $O$ of $(a_0,a_2,\ldots,a_{M-2})$ and $(a_1,a_3,\ldots,a_{M-1})$, using the primitive root $\omega^2$. For $0\le k<M/2$, return $\widehat a_k=E_k+\omega^k O_k$ and $\widehat a_{k+M/2}=E_k-\omega^kO_k$. The inverse transform is obtained by running the same procedure with $\overline\omega$ and dividing every output by $M$.

Thus each output uses only the input sites in its receptive field, mixes input channels by matrix multiplication, and uses the same weights and bias at every output site. source_lines.28: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, so the usual Lebesgue-measurable sets on $\mathbb R$ form a complete measure space with Lebesgue measure $\lambda$. Every bounded interval is Lebesgue measurable, and any interval is the countable union of its bounded intersections with $[-n,n]$; since the Lebesgue-measurable sets form a sigma-algebra, $I$ is measurable and $\lambda$ restricts to $I$. Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with $t_0\in I$, and let $N,m,p\ge1$ be finite. A continuous-time linear state-space model consists of matrices $A\in\mathbb F^{N\times N}$, $B\in\mathbb F^{N\times m}$, $C\in\mathbb F^{p\times N}$, $D\in\mathbb F^{p\times m}$, an initial value $x_0\in\mathbb F^N$, and an input $u:I\to\mathbb F^m$ whose real and imaginary coordinates are Lebesgue measurable and integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$. A state trajectory is a function $x:I\to\mathbb F^N$ whose real and imaginary coordinates are absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $I$ (with absolute continuity defined by the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ condition on finite families of disjoint subintervals), with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$ outside a Lebesgue-null subset of $I$. Its output is $y(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t)$. The term $Du(t)$ is the direct input-to-output term and is separate from the state contribution $Cx(t)$.

source_lines.61: [F1] [[def-message-passing-gnn]]: Each layer applies the same aggregation function to the multiset of neighbor states and then the same update function to the center state and aggregate.
source_lines.63: [F2] [[def-one-dimensional-weisfeiler-lehman-test]]: Each next WL color is the ordered pair of the current color and the multiset of current neighbor colors; the graph color multiset records every vertex color with multiplicity.
source_lines.71: 1.1 By induction on $t=0,\ldots,K$, equal round-$t$ WL colors of vertices from either graph imply equal GNN states after $t$ layers. At $t=0$, the shared initial embedding gives this implication. If it holds at $t$ and two vertices have equal round-$(t+1)$ colors, [F2] says their center colors and neighbor-color multisets agree. By the induction hypothesis, equal neighbor colors have equal GNN states; applying this correspondence occurrence by occurrence gives equal neighbor-state multisets. The shared aggregation and update functions in [F1] therefore give equal next-layer states. Thus a well-defined map from each round-$t$ color occurring in either graph to its common GNN state exists. [given, F1, F2, induction, algebra]
source_lines.73: 2.1 At round $K$, the assumed equal WL color multisets become equal multisets of GNN states when each color is sent to its common state from step 1.1; multiplicities are preserved by [F3]. The shared graph readout in [F4] receives equal multisets, so the two graph outputs are equal. The contrapositive gives the stated distinguishing implication. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.31: Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. source_lines.41: [F1] [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]]: a finite topologically ordered program has a scalar output, and repeated parent slots are separate uses in its dependency graph.
source_lines.43: [F2] [[alg-backpropagation-through-shared-parameter-recurrence]]: the forward pass computes $h_0,\ldots,h_T$; the reverse pass initializes the loss cotangent, adds each transition's parameter pullback to the same parameter accumulator, propagates the state cotangent backward, and finally pulls back through $h_0$.
source_lines.45: [F3] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: on a finite $C^1$ program and fixed strict branch, reverse mode returns the exact derivative transpose of its scalar output.
source_lines.47: [F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable finite-dimensional maps, the total derivative of a composition is the ordered composition of their total derivatives.
